extracted.intended_audience: general readers, social reformers, journalists, and policymakers interested in late-19th-century urban housing and public health
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic/social‑reform study of tenement-house conditions in New York City (late 19th century), documenting causes, statistics, public-health impacts, and recommended remedies. The work aims to describe, diagnose, and motivate remedial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal definition of 'tenement'
rubrics_metrics.description: The law defines it as a house "occupied by three or more families, living independently and doing their cooking on the premises; or by more than two families on a floor, so living and cooking and having a common right in the halls, stairways, yards, etc."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal meaning includes flats and apartment-houses (though the author excludes such from discussion in the narrower sense). It establishes the statutory threshold for what constitutes a tenement and whom regulation targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of light and ventilation (windows and air-shafts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interior rooms must have provision or possibility for the admission of light and air; dark bedrooms and unventilated rooms are condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board of Health ordered cutting of more than forty-six thousand windows in interior rooms (1869). The 'era of the air-shaft' is presented as a sanitary improvement for new houses, though many old houses remain unventilated. Example: many living-rooms and bedrooms in older tenements had little or no access to light/air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/closure of cellar dwellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellars used as living apartments are unacceptable housing and should be closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five hundred and fifty cellars south of Houston Street were closed after enforcement; in many instances police had to forcibly remove tenants. Cellars below tide-water and underground lodging-houses are cited as particularly dangerous and unsanitary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on overcrowding / acceptable occupancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme overcrowding (many persons per small room) is a defining and condemnable feature of tenement life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author documents examples (e.g., one room 12 × 12 with five families totaling twenty persons; tenements with 101 adults and 91 children). Overcrowding is repeatedly linked to ill-health, moral decay, and juvenile crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners' duty of maintenance: repairs, cleanliness, and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors are responsible for keeping tenement premises in repair, clean, and orderly; negligence is a primary cause of squalor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book cites owners' excuses blaming tenants' filthy habits but stresses that tolerance of such habits and failure to repair are owners' responsibility. Agents' instructions to 'collect the rent in advance, or, failing, eject the occupants' exemplify profit-driven neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural safety and sound foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings must be erected or altered with regard to the strength of foundation walls and general structural safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice of carrying up old buildings 'without regard to the strength of the foundation walls' is presented as hazardous; exemplified by rear-houses and additions that compromised safety for rent income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of 'rear houses' and multiple-dwelling conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion of rear houses, stables, shops, or other structures into human dwellings or barracks is unsafe and unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author documents how rear houses, old churches, stables, and shops were converted into overcrowded dwellings (e.g., 40 families in a former church), producing extremely high mortality rates and unsanitary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary law control of new tenement construction
rubrics_metrics.description: New tenement construction should be subject to sanitary law (air-shafts, ventilation, limits on dark rooms) to prevent perpetuation of old evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While sanitary law exercises 'full control' over new houses (the air-shaft era), existing old tenements remain a problem. The implication is that standards must be enforced on new construction to improve overall conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground area / lot allotment per capita
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a reasonable pro rata allotment of ground area per person; extreme crowding of people on a lot is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters testified to lots where pro rata ground area was 'scarcely equal to two square yards upon the city lot, court-yards and all included.' Such figures are used to argue for the untenability and danger of current densities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link housing quality to public health and crime metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate tenements by their measurable public-health outcomes (mortality rates, epidemic spread) and social outcomes (juvenile crime, pauperism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book cites specific statistics (e.g., mortality rates rising, cholera vulnerability, 'tenants died at the rate of one hundred and ninety-five to the thousand' in Gotham Court) and links poor housing conditions to the production of criminals, paupers, tramps, and charity dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic standard: critique of profit-maximizing ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess tenement practices in light of owners seeking high percentages on outlay (commonly 15–30% and sometimes 100%) that encourage neglect and speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that tenement evils are systemically produced by the profit motive; recommends that employers build homes for workers and that capital which created the evil must help undo it. The phrase 'Philanthropy and five per cent.' is used critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-policy remedy: provision of clean, comfortable homes to prevent social ills
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventive social policy should aim to provide every man with a clean and comfortable home as a means to curb drunkenness and other social ills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites a legislative committee's conclusion recommending prevention of drunkenness by providing clean comfortable homes; author uses this as policy guidance linking housing reform to moral and social improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of saloons and evasion of laws in tenement premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Retail alcohol outlets and practices that evade regulation (e.g., side doors to serve inmates and dodge Sunday laws) are targets for regulation within tenement contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes first-floor stores used for liquor with side openings for inmates to evade Sunday law; such practices compound tenement social problems and require enforcement.
